name: Eye yoga / eye exercises

lead: Eye yoga is a set of routines built from eye movements, palming and focus shifting. Practitioners, including some in looksmaxxing circles, say it eases strain and firms or brightens the skin around the eyes.

The practice descends from the Bates method, developed by William Horatio Bates (1860-1931). The proposed path is less strain and more tone in the surrounding muscles. Reviews of eye exercises for vision, including a 2005 review of 43 studies, reported no clear benefit for visual acuity, and no study has tested an effect on how the eye area looks.

paras: People spend a few minutes a day moving their eyes in circles and directions, shifting focus near and far, and resting covered palms over closed eyes. It is usually done at a desk or before bed, and people describe it as a relaxation habit rather than a quick change.

Plain eye movements are low-risk. Related Bates-method practices such as sungazing or pressing on the eyes have documented risks, and dropping prescribed glasses can be unsafe, especially when driving.

web.title: Computer usage and your eyes - AAO

angle.text: Practitioners use eye movements, palming and focus shifting to relieve strain, with the hope of a firmer, brighter eye area. Reviews have studied eye exercises for vision, and an appearance effect has not been tested.

lead: Eye yoga, or eye exercises, is a family of routines made up of deliberate eye movements, palming, focus shifting, blinking drills and relaxation. In looksmaxxing circles, practitioners use it with the aim of relaxing the muscles around the eyes, easing the squinting or tired expression that long screen sessions can produce, and keeping the eye area looking open, rested and bright. The practice draws on a lineage that includes the Bates method, an alternative therapy developed by the American eye doctor William Horatio Bates (1860-1931), together with yoga-inspired eye routines and Chinese school eye exercises.[1][2]

Proponents describe a chain in which relaxed eyes and less strain lead to a more open, rested expression and a fresher-looking periorbital area. The routines need no equipment and take a few minutes, which is part of their appeal for people who work at screens. Research on eye exercises concerns vision, eye-movement disorders, sports performance and balance; no published study has measured them against the appearance of the skin or tissues around the eyes.[3][4][5]

Reviews of vision training for eyesight itself, including a 2004 American Academy of Ophthalmology review and a 2005 review of 43 studies, report no clear improvement in visual acuity.[1] Orthoptic eye exercises are, however, an established part of clinical care for some eye-movement disorders such as convergence problems and double vision after neurological injury.[4][5] For screen-related eye comfort, the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends regular breaks to look at distant objects and conscious blinking.[6]
infobox: Palming, shifting and swinging the gaze, focus changes, blinking, eye rolling
Firmer, brighter, more rested eye area

paras: Techniques associated with the Bates method include palming (covering closed eyes with the palms without pressure), visualising small black letters or dots, and shifting or swinging the gaze.[1] Modern eye yoga routines commonly combine these with eye rolling, near-and-far focusing and blinking exercises, and are often promoted for people who spend long periods at screens.

Related clinical and sports routines exist under other names. Orthoptic exercises such as pencil push-ups and the Brock string are used in vision therapy, and athletes use focus-flip and ball-on-a-string drills to practise visual skills.[3][4][7]

Chinese eye exercises are a separate tradition: a school routine of gentle acupoint massage around the eyes, performed daily by schoolchildren, that has been described in the paediatric ophthalmology literature since at least 1980.[2][8]

The looks rationale offered by practitioners is that tension and fatigue around the eyes show as squinting, tired-looking lids and a drawn eye area, and that relaxing and exercising the eyes counters this. The idea parallels facial-exercise routines for other areas of the face, and routines are often combined with warm-palm compresses, blinking reminders and screen breaks.

Everyday eye comfort is a related thread. The American Academy of Ophthalmology notes that people blink about 15 times a minute normally but only about 5 to 7 times while using screens, and advises conscious blinking and periodic focus on distant objects to relieve strain, aches and dryness.[6] Practitioners of eye yoga fold similar habits into their routines, with the aim of looking less fatigued.
No published trial has measured under-eye puffiness, lid position, wrinkles or skin firmness after eye exercises, so these effects are described by practitioners rather than documented in studies.

Bates held that mental strain made the muscles around the eyeball distort its shape, and that relieving the strain could correct refractive errors; he rejected the mainstream account in which the ciliary muscle inside the eye changes the lens's curvature.[1] He referred to glasses as crutches and recommended discarding them.[1]

Bates also advised 'sunning', brief exposure of the closed eyelids, and for a time the white of the eye, to sunlight; posthumous editions of his book dropped the open-eye advice.[1] Palming was described as producing 'illusions' of light and colour, which sceptics attribute to the brain's background neural activity (eigengrau).[1]

Variants continue to circulate. Wikipedia describes a Swedish self-published programme, John Slavicek's Yoga for the Eyes, that combined Bates ideas with yogic eye exercises and claimed improved sight in three days; an evaluating ophthalmologist rejected it, and the WHO and St. Erik's Eye Foundation showed no interest because no double-blind tests had been conducted.[1]

Bates reported in 1891 in the New York Medical Journal that he had reversed seven cases of myopia, and in 1911 he claimed to teach myopic schoolchildren to focus at a distance.[1] In 1917 he partnered with Bernarr Macfadden on a heavily advertised correspondence course that the American Medical Association's investigation bureau criticised; in 1919 he began the magazine Better Eyesight, and in 1920 he self-published Perfect Sight Without Glasses.[1] In 1929 the US Federal Trade Commission filed a complaint over misleading advertising.[1]

After Bates died in 1931, his widow Emily and associates continued the work. Gayelord Hauser published an endorsing book in 1932 that added his own exercises and dietary products.[1] Aldous Huxley, who took lessons from teacher Margaret Darst Corbett in 1939, popularised the approach in The Art of Seeing (1942); he later needed a magnifying glass to read a memorised speech.[1] In 1940 Corbett and an assistant were charged in California with practising medicine without a licence, and a jury returned a not-guilty verdict.[1]

Critical assessments followed: in 1952 optometry professor Elwin Marg wrote that most of Bates's claims and almost all of his theories had been considered false by practically all visual scientists, and in 1956 optometrist Philip Pollack published The Truth about Eye Exercises.[1] In 2006 sales of the See Clearly Method, which used Bates-derived techniques, were halted by a court order over dishonest marketing.[1] Chinese school eye exercises, a different tradition involving acupoint massage, have been taught to schoolchildren since the 1960s and are among interventions recommended in China's myopia-prevention plan.[2]

Laboratory measurements published in 1998 found that the eyeball changes length only minutely during focusing, far less than the Bates theory required.[1] The American Academy of Ophthalmology review found no objective evidence that visual training improves eyesight and attributed reported gains to factors such as better interpretation of blurred images, mood or the pinhole effect of the pupil.[1] Blur adaptation, in which perception adjusts to life without lenses, is also offered as an explanation for some reported improvements.[1]

Critics note the method is hard to test, because relaxation and imagination are difficult to verify and a placebo trial is hard to design.[1] A 2023 systematic review of interventions recommended in China for children's myopia found that time outdoors and reduced near work lowered new myopia, and that all interventions had a limited effect on progression; eye exercises were among those assessed.[2]

On screens, the American Academy of Ophthalmology states that the belief that screens permanently damage the eyes is untrue, and describes screen-related strain as similar to that from other close work such as reading or sewing.[6]

Commentators on the Bates method note that sungazing can injure the eye, pressing on the eyeballs while palming may raise glaucoma risk, and abandoning corrective lenses can be unsafe, for example when driving, or can delay treatment of conditions such as glaucoma or amblyopia in children.[1] Gentle movements and palming without pressure are not associated with reported harms.
No studies found for eye exercises as a means of changing the appearance of the eye area.

Related research covers other uses. Reviews describe eye muscle exercises as part of treatment for eye-movement disorders and diplopia after neurological damage,[4][5] and a 2023 review assessed Chinese eye exercises among myopia-prevention measures with limited effects on progression.[2] Vision training for visual acuity has not shown clear benefit.[1]

Studies of eye exercises as therapy exist in other settings. Reviews describe non-surgical management of ophthalmoplegia and neurologic diplopia and the role of vision therapy and orthoptics,[4][5][7] and randomised trials have examined orthoptic exercise regimes in young adults and gaze-stability exercises in older adults with dizziness.[9][10] A 2025 randomised trial of Chinese acupoint eye exercises in 55 participants (110 eyes) compared standard, sham, eye-closure and distance-looking groups on ocular vascular parameters after near work; the publication has since been retracted.[11]

lore.intro: Eye yoga is discussed in appearance circles mainly as a free, equipment-free way to look less tired and to counter screen strain; its claims descend from the Bates method and are mostly discussed through that lineage.[1][6]

claims.claim: Eye exercises relax the muscles around the eyes and make the eyes look more open and rested.
Palming and relaxation can improve eyesight and reduce the need for glasses.
Reduced blinking at screens drives tired-looking eyes, and blinking drills help.
Sunning, brief sunlight exposure on the closed eye, energises and heals the eyes.
Eye exercises prevent or slow myopia in children.
Eye exercises have a legitimate medical form.
